title: Epilepsy surgery for temporal lobe seizures
description: When temporal lobe seizures cannot be controlled with medicine, surgery to remove or disconnect the area where they start can stop them; about two thirds of people become seizure-free. One study scanned people before and, on average, more than three years after surgery. In those who became seizure-free, the brainstem's arousal centres, which keep the brain awake and alert, became more in step again with the cortex. Lines show how closely areas work together: in the first part compared with people without epilepsy (dashed means less); in "What changed" compared with before surgery (pulsing means more).
caveat: All findings come from one study of 15 people with temporal lobe epilepsy, 10 of whom became seizure-free after surgery, and 15 people without epilepsy. In the 5 who still had seizures, nothing changed. The surgery itself, removing part of the temporal lobe, is not drawn. The arousal centres studied are small nuclei in the upper brainstem and the ventral tegmental area; they are drawn as the brainstem outline, and "frontal" neocortex is drawn on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which are approximations. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before surgery, the brainstem arousal centres are less in step with the cortex than in people without epilepsy.

phases.name: Surgery and recovery
phases.caption: Surgery, then at least a year (on average more than three) before the second scan. The brain is drawn at rest here.
